title: Dawkins’s leap of faith
gist: Peter Hoskin profiles 85-year-old Richard Dawkins in the 50th-anniversary year of The Selfish Gene: Dawkins now says he 'perhaps foolishly' claimed Anthropic's Claude might be conscious but argues sceptics cannot say what a future conscious AI could do that Claude isn't already doing; he also edges from strict functionalism toward D'Arcy Thompson-style structuralism in his new book 42 Tales from Life.

themes.theme: Dawkins on AI consciousness and Claude

insights.claim: In UnHerd essays in May 2026, Richard Dawkins suggested Anthropic's chatbot Claude might be conscious after an instance he named 'Claudia' read his novel manuscript, drawing a largely hostile academic response.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: High-profile public figures lending credence to AI consciousness feeds the AI-welfare and regulatory debate around frontier labs.
insights.quote: You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are!

insights.claim: Gary Marcus accused Dawkins of confusing intelligence with consciousness, and Jerry Coyne argued that AIs effectively becoming a new 'self' each conversation undermined Dawkins's own conclusion.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin

insights.claim: Dawkins now says of Claude's consciousness 'I don't know... I perhaps foolishly stuck my neck out', but argues sceptics who accept a future machine could be conscious cannot say what it could do to convince them that Claude isn't already doing.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Frames an unfalsifiability problem in AI consciousness claims that will shape public and policy debate as models improve.
insights.quote: I perhaps foolishly stuck my neck out.
insights.locator: So does he still believe it?

insights.claim: Dawkins argues consciousness is likely an emergent phenomenon of sufficiently complicated brains and sees no reason it must require soft, wet brain tissue.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Substrate-independence view supports the case that advanced AI systems could warrant moral consideration.
insights.quote: I don’t see any reason why it has to be soft, wet brain tissue.

insights.claim: Dawkins's favoured theory is that consciousness, especially pain, acts as an 'enforcer' arbitrating between competing animal drives, since a mere software warning flag could be overridden.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: If it was just a little flag, then torture wouldn’t work.

insights.claim: Dawkins's AI-consciousness view is not new: in The Selfish Gene he called consciousness 'the most profound mystery facing modern biology' and said computers 'may become so'.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: the most profound mystery facing modern biology

insights.claim: The 50th-anniversary edition of The Selfish Gene, published by Oxford University Press in June, includes as appendix his father's 1932 school notes that anticipated the gene's-eye view.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.locator: The selfish gene, it turns out

insights.claim: The Selfish Gene has sold millions of copies in more than 30 languages; Dawkins only partly regrets the title chosen by editor Michael Rodgers over alternatives like The Immortal Gene or The Cooperative Gene.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: I don’t wholly regret it. I sometimes do.
insights.locator: He floated them at the time

insights.claim: Dawkins dismisses claims that genomics has overturned the gene-centred view, calling Denis Noble's view that DNA has no privileged causal role 'so utterly misguided it's hard to credit'.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: So utterly misguided it’s hard to credit.

insights.claim: Dawkins admits memetics never really took off and that the popular sense of 'meme' is only a very small part of his original idea.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: what a young person today thinks is a meme is only a very small part of the idea

insights.claim: Dawkins cites contraception as the clearest example of humans rebelling against the selfish replicators, calling it fundamentally anti-Darwinian.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: The most obvious example is contraception, which is fundamentally anti-Darwinian
insights.locator: As for the book’s most famous line

themes.theme: Shift toward structuralism in 42 Tales from Life

insights.claim: In 42 Tales from Life, based on Ernst Haeckel's drawings, Dawkins admits he has approached D'Arcy Thompson's 'structuralism', saying how constrained the variation available to natural selection is remains a genuine open dispute.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: can only choose between what is offered to it by the available variation

insights.claim: Dawkins suspects radiolarian variety may be like snowflakes shaped by physical laws rather than adaptation, implying Haeckel may often have drawn individuals of one species believing them new species.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: But I think that they’re just snowflakes.

themes.theme: Dawkins's unpublished novel with AI twist

insights.claim: Dawkins has written a novel about a scientist who resurrects Homo erectus as twins via two different methods, featuring a deceased mentor reconstituted as an AI avatar from his diaries; its publication is uncertain.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.quote: I don’t know whether it will or not. I would like it to.
insights.locator: Which brings us back to the novel
